extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, revenue officers, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical guidance for designing and assessing taxes on land, produce, houses, and ground-rents, with attention to administration, incidence, equity, and economic incentives. Draws on historical examples (Prussia, Bohemia, Holland, China, Bengal, England) to illustrate consequences of different tax bases and collection methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative cost and ease of collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of collecting a tax should be moderate and ideally much below what is incurred in levying other taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that some systems (e.g., a register of leases) may keep collection costs low, while full surveys and valuations are laborious and expensive (e.g., Domesday-like surveys). High collection costs reduce the net revenue and may make a tax impractical. Example: payment in kind leads to greater losses by collectors and greater abuse than money payments; mandarins and tax-gatherers in China have an incentive to maintain in-kind collection because it is more easily abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding discouragement of improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax should not discourage landlords or farmers from improving land or adopting valuable crops and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A variable land-tax that shares profit of improvements with the sovereign may make landlords less disposed to improve. Proposed remedy: allow the landlord, before improving, to ascertain value jointly with revenue officers and be rated for a number of years sufficient to indemnify him. Smith notes that no sovereign’s vague interest can counterbalance discouraging a landlord’s direct interest; policy should prioritize leaving landlords and farmers free to pursue their own interest to encourage cultivation and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation/indemnification for improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a tax could capture returns to improvements, provide a mechanism allowing proprietors to ascertain valuation and be exempted or rated for a sufficient indemnification period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith suggests equitable arbitration by local landlords and farmers, jointly chosen, to fix a valuation and rate the proprietor for a term long enough to fully indemnify improvement expense. Term should not be longer than necessary (to avoid remoteness of sovereign interest), but better somewhat too long than too short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aligning sovereign incentives toward public improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax systems that make the sovereign’s revenue depend on increased produce can motivate the state to promote infrastructure and market access that raise land value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith cites Asian examples (China, Bengal under Muhammadans, ancient Egypt) where taxes on produce led sovereigns to maintain roads and canals to increase quantity and value of produce. He contrasts this with church tithes, whose fragmented proprietors lack incentive to invest in public improvements, producing less beneficial outcomes for cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and self-adjustment versus continual revaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer tax forms that adapt to changes in society and produce without requiring perpetual government revaluation and intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tax proportional to the current rent/produce will 'readily suit itself to the actual situation of things' and be equally just through variations in agriculture, silver value, and coin standard. By contrast, taxes fixed by an initial survey or valuation become unequal over a moderate period and require continual, painful attention or arbitrary additional levies (example: Montauban’s additional tax and application by intendant discretion). Smith recommends establishing such adaptable taxes as perpetual/fundamental laws rather than recurring uncertain assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register of leases preferred to full survey where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, use a register of leases rather than an expensive, frequent, and intrusive full survey and valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full surveys (e.g., Prussian, Bohemian, Milanese surveys) are accurate but costly and require ongoing review. Registers reduce cost and complexity and may mitigate collusion concerns more practically than state-wide surveys; Smith notes some states used surveys because of fear of lessor/lessee collusion, but a simple lease register is a simpler expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ad hoc corrective levies based on outdated assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on applying arbitrary additional taxes to correct inequalities caused by obsolete valuations, because such corrections are often arbitrary and discretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Montauban (1666 assessment later unequal; additional tax of 1727 rated on old assessment but levied only on under-charged districts to relieve overcharged ones). Smith criticizes the arbitrariness of intendant discretion in such remedies and the administrative unfairness that can result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of incidence: produce taxes ultimately fall on landlords
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes levied on the produce of land are, in reality, taxes upon the rent, and though originally advanced by the farmer, are finally paid by the landlord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers anticipate a produce-based tax and bargain lower rent to cover it. The tithe example: if a tenth is taken, farmers demand rent abatements, reducing landlord rent. Policy design must therefore track who ultimately bears tax burdens (farmers vs landlords) and not assume nominal payer equals final payer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taxing a fixed share of produce when it produces extreme inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes that take a fixed portion of produce (tithes) are unequal across lands since a given share of produce corresponds to very different shares of rent in rich vs poor land, and so are highly regressive for poorer soils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith demonstrates with numerical examples: in very fertile land where half the produce replaces farmer’s capital, a tenth tithe reduces landlord’s share from 5/10 to 4/10; in poor land where four-fifths replaces farmer’s capital, the same tithe reduces landlord’s share much more severely. Such taxes discourage expensive improvements and valuable crops (e.g., madder) unless exempted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of produce-based taxes can incentivize public investment if revenue funds the state
rubrics_metrics.description: If the produce-based tax funds the state (not private ecclesiastical proprietors), it can incentivize rulers to invest in roads, canals, and markets that increase produce and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes Asian sovereigns taxed produce and then maintained infrastructure to increase markets; when taxes funded the church, which did not reinvest in public improvement, the tax only caused harm without promoting cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer monetary taxation to in-kind collection where practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment in kind (collecting actual produce) is more liable to mismanagement and abuse in collection; monetary payments reduce these abuses and are preferable for larger-scale public revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small, local recipients (parson, small gentleman) in-kind payments may be practical because they can oversee collection, but for sovereign revenue the losses from collectors’ abuse would be much greater. Smith notes some Chinese provinces still paid in kind and that collectors have incentives to continue such practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: When money taxes are used, prefer market-varying valuation to fixed commodity valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A money tax based on a valuation that varies with market prices will keep the tax's produce-equivalence proportional to real produce value; fixed valuations cause the tax to diverge from real value with changes in metal content or commodity prices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a bushel of wheat is always rated at a fixed money price, the tax's produce-equivalence will vary with precious metal value and coin standard. A valuation tied to current market prices keeps the tax proportionate to actual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-money 'modus' payments are neutral with respect to improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A fixed sum in money in lieu of tithes becomes like a land tax that neither rises nor falls with rent and therefore neither encourages nor discourages improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith cites Bengal under Mahometan government where a moderate modus (fixed sum) replaced in-kind fifths; such moduses are neutral toward improvement but, if changed back to in-kind under poor management, can discourage cultivation and open abuse (example under East India Company servants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish building-rent from ground-rent when taxing house rents
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate building-rent (return on capital invested in building and repair) from ground-rent (surplus paid for situation advantage); tax design should avoid burdening building-rent but can target ground-rent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building-rent must be enough to pay ordinary interest and replace capital; taxing it risks discouraging builders. Ground-rent is largely an unearned monopoly return attributable to location and public governance and can better bear peculiar taxation without discouraging industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax incidence on house-rent affects inhabitants differently by income class
rubrics_metrics.description: A proportional tax on house-rent payable by tenants will, in general, fall more heavily on the rich (house-rent a larger share of luxury expenses) and affect different classes unevenly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith explains that the proportion of house-rent to total living expense is higher for the rich and lower for the poor; thus a house-rent tax may be progressive (falls heavier on rich) and this may be reasonable. However, effects differ across circumstances and the poor’s necessities limit their ability to substitute away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taxing uninhabited houses or taxable subjects that yield no income to proprietor
rubrics_metrics.description: Houses not inhabited ought to pay no tax, because such a tax would fall entirely on the proprietor for a subject affording neither convenience nor revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith criticizes taxation of uninhabited houses (e.g., Holland case where every house taxed at 2.5% of value regardless of occupation). In many English districts untenanted houses are exempted by assessors; taxing uninhabited property can be especially harsh where market interest rates make the tax a high fraction of building-rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose tax bases that minimize intrusive inspection and be externally verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax bases that can be measured without entering dwellings (e.g., number of windows) are less offensive than those requiring intrusive visits (e.g., hearth-money), but they may still be unequal in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearth-money required entering every room (odious); window counts can be done from the outside and are less offensive. Yet such measures (window-tax) still have inequality problems and may be regressive, and Smith notes successive alterations to window and dwelling taxes illustrate tradeoffs between administrative convenience and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware regressivity and unequal burden from ostensibly simple bases (hearth/window taxes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, observable proxies for ability to pay (hearths, windows) often produce inequality of the worst kind by falling disproportionately on the poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that such taxes frequently fall heavier on the poor than the rich despite appearing proportional to house size; the principal objection to these taxes is their inequality. Historical changes in English dwelling/window taxes demonstrate how these measures can become odious and be repealed or altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground-rents are especially appropriate for peculiarly taxing unearned advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground-rents — surplus beyond building-rent arising from situation and public governance — are proper subjects for peculiar taxation because they do not discourage productive industry and reflect benefits of good government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax on ground-rent will not raise house rents because competitors’ wealth is not increased by taxation; final payment falls on ground owner acting as monopolist. Smith reasons that ground-rents owe existence to good government and so it is reasonable they contribute more than many other funds to state support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to distinguish ground-rent from building-rent in assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Although contrivers of taxes have found difficulty distinguishing ground- and building-rent, Smith contends it should not be very difficult and the distinction is important for fair tax design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to separate the two parts leads to taxing returns that are the builder’s ordinary profit (discouraging building) rather than the unearned site value. Smith points to practical assessment methods (valuation of what a house would fetch if let; exempting uninhabited houses) and historical practice differences across countries (Great Britain’s land tax vs Holland’s value tax) as relevant considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider local interest rates and valuation timing when setting tax rates on house value
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax rate that may be burdensome in a low market-interest environment (e.g., 2.5% when interest is 3%) can consume a large part of building-rent and be ruinous to proprietors if based on building cost rather than letting value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes Holland’s tax at 2.5% of house value may amount to more than a third of building-rent where market interest is 3%. He warns that rating inhabited proprietor’s houses according to building expense rather than probable letting rent would be ruinous at modest tax rates, because accumulated multi-generational expense has low exchangeable value.
